title: India Just Built Its First Military Aircraft. A Private Company Did It Months Ahead of Schedule.
excerpt: The Tata-Airbus C-295 completed its maiden flight from Vadodara on June 10, making it the first military aircraft ever manufactured in India by a private-sector company — with 85% of the structure built by Indian MSMEs.
body:
On June 10, a twin-engine turboprop lifted off from a production line in Gujarat that did not exist three years ago. It was not the first C-295 to fly in Indian skies. But it was the first one *built* there — and that distinction carries enormous weight.

The aircraft, assembled by **Tata Advanced Systems Limited (TASL)** in partnership with **Airbus Defence and Space** at a dedicated Final Assembly Line (FAL) in Vadodara, completed its maiden test flight, marking the first time a private-sector Indian company has manufactured a full military aircraft. It came in months ahead of its original September 2026 deadline.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted the milestone during the 135th episode of *Mann Ki Baat*, calling the C-295 a symbol of India becoming "increasingly secure and self-reliant."

## The Deal Behind the Aircraft

In 2021, India signed a ₹21,935 crore ($2.6 billion) contract with Airbus for 56 C-295 medium transport aircraft to replace the Indian Air Force's ageing fleet of Avro Hawker Siddeley HS748s — workhorses that entered service over six decades ago.

Under the deal, the first 16 aircraft were supplied directly from Airbus's facility in Seville, Spain, and have already been delivered to the IAF. The remaining 40 are being built entirely in India at the Vadodara facility.

"This maiden test flight is a crucial step in the aircraft's post-production testing process," Airbus said. "As the first of 40 aircraft to be built in India, the test flight advances the programme's objective of delivering the first made-in-India C-295 aircraft this year."

## What "Made in India" Actually Means

The C-295 programme is not screwdriver assembly. According to Airbus, over **85% of the structural assembly** involves parts manufactured across a localised supply network of Indian micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). Components are transported to the Vadodara facility from across the country.

The production line employs Indian engineers and technicians trained by Airbus, and the longer-term ambition is to develop the facility into a regional hub for C-295 production — including potential export orders.

The aircraft itself, registration CA 7117, flew without its final coat of paint but carried the IAF's roundel and tail flash. It will now undergo the full certification process before being handed over to the Indian Air Force later this year.

## A Broader Defence Manufacturing Moment

The C-295 milestone comes during a month that Modi described in *Mann Ki Baat* as one where India proved it was becoming secure "from the seas to the skies":

- **Three indigenous warships** — INS Dunagiri, INS Sanshodhak and INS Agray — were inducted into the Indian Navy in Kolkata, all designed and manufactured domestically.
- The **DRDO successfully tested its Long-Range Land Attack Cruise Missile (LRLACM)** on June 15, an indigenously developed weapon with an estimated range of 1,000–1,500 km. Senior officials from both the Indian Navy and the Air Force witnessed the launch, signalling its positioning as a tri-service asset.
- Earlier in the month, DRDO demonstrated **multi-layered ballistic missile defence capability**, putting India in an elite group of nations able to engage threats up to intercontinental ballistic missile range.

## What Comes Next

The C-295 programme is separate from India's larger Medium Transport Aircraft effort, which is seeking 60–80 aircraft to replace Soviet-era Il-76 and An-32 military airlifters. Airbus is expected to compete for that contract using its A400M platform.

For now, the Vadodara assembly line will continue producing C-295s for the IAF, and Airbus has flagged interest from other countries — potentially making India an export base for a European military aircraft, a reversal that would have seemed implausible a decade ago.

The IAF congratulated the entire team: "The achievement reinforces India's growing aerospace capabilities and underscores the Indian Air Force's commitment to fostering indigenous defence capability under the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat."

For a country long tagged as the world's largest arms importer, the sight of a military transport aircraft lifting off from an Indian private-sector assembly line — months ahead of schedule — is more than a procurement milestone. It is an industrial argument, made in metal and propeller wash.
